Learning Objectives
Identify clinical manifestations of acromioclavicular joint separation, acromioclavicular
osteoarthritis, and distal clavicle osteolysis.
Review the differential diagnosis for acromioclavicular joint pain.
Describe the Rockwood classification of acromioclavicular joint separation.
Discuss nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for the management of traumatic
acromioclavicular joint conditions.
Discuss nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for the management of degenerative
acromioclavicular joint conditions.

Overview

Overview
Acromioclavicular joint pathology is commonly indicated by the radiographic
degeneration of the acromioclavicular joint; however, this finding is not necessarily
symptomatic. Acromioclavicular joint pain may be related to trauma, acromioclavicular
separation, distal clavicle osteolysis, osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, or septic
arthritis. Acromioclavicular separation is the most common traumatic condition of the
acromioclavicular joint, and osteoarthritis and distal clavicle osteolysis are the most
common degenerative conditions of the acromioclavicular joint.1
Epidemiology
Traumatic Conditions of the Acromioclavicular Joint: Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Common injury that may be acute or chronic
Accounts for approximately 12% of all shoulder injuries observed in clinical practice and
contributes to approximately one-half of all shoulder injuries in contact athletes2
Atraumatic and Degenerative Conditions of the Acromioclavicular Joint
Osteoarthritis
Most common pathology of the acromioclavicular joint3
More common with advanced age after degeneration of the intra-articular disk
Arthritic degeneration can begin in middle age and is not always symptomatic.
More common in patients engaging in repetitive overhead or lifting activities
Previous acromioclavicular joint separations may result in earlier and more progressive
acromioclavicular arthritis.
The radiographic severity of arthritis does not always correlate with patient symptoms, and
many affected patients are asymptomatic.
Distal Clavicle Osteolysis

More common in active male patients in their twenties and thirties; however, an increase
recently has been reported in young female patients because of the increased popularity of
female body building.4,5
Associated with heavy weightlifting or repetitive motions
Relatively uncommon, occurring in approximately 6% of young patients with acromioclavicular
joint pain5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Bones
The acromioclavicular joint is formed between the lateral end of the clavicle and the medial
end of the acromion.
The distal clavicle epiphysis fuses at a late age, between 18 and 22 years.
Vasculature
The acromioclavicular joint is supplied by two arteries.
Suprascapular artery, arising from the subclavian artery at the thyrocervical trunk
Thoraco-acromial artery, arising from the axillary artery
Nerves
The acromioclavicular joint is innervated by branches of three nerves.
Lateral pectoral
Suprascapular
Axillary
Joints and Ligaments
Acromioclavicular joint anatomy
The acromioclavicular joint is a diarthrodial joint separated by a fibrocartilaginous disk.
The angle of inclination of the distal clavicle and acromial facet articular surfaces is highly
variable.
The acromioclavicular joint capsule surrounds the joint and is reinforced on all sides by the
acromioclavicular joint capsule ligaments.

Coracoclavicular ligament anatomy (Figure 1; Resource 1)
The coracoclavicular ligaments consist of trapezoid (anterolateral) and conoid (posteromedial)
ligaments that are major vertical stabilizers of the acromioclavicular joint.
Trapezoid ligament
The larger of the two and quadrilateral in shape
Inserts at the inferior and distal clavicle in a region 1.5 to 3.0 mm medial from the
acromioclavicular joint6
Restrains posterior clavicular displacement and acromioclavicular joint compression6
Conoid ligament
Is conical in shape
Originates from the conoid tubercle on the clavicle
Connects posteromedial to the trapezoid ligament6
Is the principal restraint to superior translation of the clavicle6

Illustration shows the acromioclavicular joint. Static stabilizers include the acromioclavicular
capsule and the coracoclavicular ligaments, consisting of the trapezoid ligament laterally and

Acromioclavicular joint biomechanics
The clavicle rotates with elevation of the shoulder; however, very little rotation is observed at
the acromioclavicular joint.
The horizontal stability of the clavicle is provided by the acromioclavicular joint ligaments.
The vertical stability of the clavicle is provided by the acromioclavicular joint ligaments and
the coracoclavicular ligaments.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The acromioclavicular joint is a synovial diarthrodial joint separated by a
fibrocartilaginous disk that degenerates with age, causing acromioclavicular arthritis. The
angle of inclination of the distal clavicle and acromial facet articular surfaces is highly
variable, ranging from near vertical to 50° of angulation of the superolateral clavicle over
the acromial facet. The clavicle rotates posteriorly 40° to 45° with full elevation of the
shoulder; however, only 5° to 8° of rotation occurs at the acromioclavicular joint because
of the synchronous upward rotation of the scapula and sternoclavicular joint motion.
The horizontal stability of the clavicle is provided by the acromioclavicular joint
ligaments, especially the superior ligaments (50%) (the posterior ligaments provide 25%).
In addition, the vertical stability of the clavicle is provided by the acromioclavicular joint
ligaments at physiologic loads and by the coracoclavicular ligaments at higher loads. The
medially positioned conoid ligament is the strongest and most important vertical
stabilizer of the acromioclavicular joint at higher loads.6 The conoid ligament inserts into
the conoid tubercle at the posteroinferior clavicle, centered at a mean of 46 mm from
the lateral end of the clavicle. The laterally positioned trapezoid ligament provides
restraint against posterolateral translation of the clavicle in relation to the coracoid and
vertical stability.6 The trapezoid ligament inserts at the undersurface of the clavicle,
centered at a mean of 25 mm from the lateral end of the clavicle. Minimal (5 and 10 mm)
resection of the distal clavicle increases the horizontal motion of the clavicle in cadaver

models, and additional translation is observed with release of the superior and posterior

Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Pathoanatomy—Injury results in progressive disruption of the ligamentous support of the
acromioclavicular joint, beginning with the capsular ligaments and progressing to the
coracoclavicular ligaments.
The extent of the acromioclavicular joint capsule and coracoclavicular ligament involvement
determines the amount of displacement of the clavicle and the entire shoulder girdle after
acromioclavicular separation and has been the basis for classification and management of
these injuries.
Osteoarthritis
Pathology—Transmission of large axial loads through the small contact area of the
acromioclavicular joint leads to repetitive microtrauma and the development of arthritis.
Most common pathology of the acromioclavicular joint
Ubiquitously observed on imaging studies but most often asymptomatic
Distal Clavicle Osteolysis
Pathology: localized hyperemia of the distal clavicle, resulting in inflammation, bone
resorption, microfractures, and secondary arthritis of the acromioclavicular joint
Risk Factors
Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Contact sports increase the risk of experiencing acromioclavicular joint separation.
Osteoarthritis
Acromioclavicular joint arthritis may be more likely in patients who engage in repetitive
overhead or lifting activities.

Patients with a history of previous low-grade acromioclavicular joint separations have a higher
risk for acromioclavicular joint arthritis.
Distal Clavicle Osteolysis
Can develop after an acute injury to the acromioclavicular joint or because of overuse in heavy
laborers or athletes involved in repetitive overhead lifting or throwing7
Bench-pressing heavy weight repetitively is strongly associated with distal clavicle osteolysis.4
Classification of Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Acromioclavicular joint separation is traditionally assessed based on the Rockwood
classification.7 (Figure 2; Table 1; Resource 2)
Type I
Acromioclavicular ligament sprain, intact coracoclavicular ligaments
Radiographs demonstrate normal coracoclavicular distance
Type II
Acromioclavicular ligament rupture, sprained but intact coracoclavicular ligaments
Radiographs demonstrate increased coracoclavicular distance (<25% compared with
contralateral side).
Type III
Disruption of the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments
Characterized by increased coracoclavicular distance
Superior displacement of the clavicle of as much as 100% of the clavicle width
Deformity is reducible
Recently, a modification of type III injuries has been proposed, consisting of type IIIA
(horizontally stable) and type IIIB (horizontally unstable).8
Type IV
Disruption of the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments, with posterior
displacement of the clavicle
Characterized by increased coracoclavicular distance
Distal clavicle is herniated into or through the deltotrapezial fascia
Deformity is not reducible.
Type V

Markedly increased coracoclavicular distance
Deformity usually not reducible because of herniation through the deltotrapezial fascia.
Type VI
Disruption of the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments, with inferior clavicle
displacement
These rare injuries result in the distal clavicle lying under the acromion or the coracoid
process.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
The mechanism of injury usually is direct trauma resulting from a fall or a direct blow on the
point of the shoulder. Indirect injuries are rare.
Osteoarthritis
Patients often report activity-related pain.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Acromioclavicular Joint Arthritis and Pathology
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000631
9/25

The pain is localized to the acromioclavicular joint, with occasional radiation anteriorly or along
the trapezius.
Pain with heavy lifting or when sleeping on the affected side also may be common patient
reports.
Distal Clavicle Osteolysis
Patients may have a history of recent acute injury to the acromioclavicular joint.
More commonly, patients have a history of repetitive overhead lifting as part of their job (such
as a laborer or farmer) or sports activity (such as weightlifting, throwing).
Physical Examination
Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Often, a prominence of the distal clavicle is present in patients with an acromioclavicular joint
separation injury; this prominence is more pronounced in patients with a higher-grade injury
(Figure 3).
Skin tenting is rare and usually is an indication of a distal clavicle fracture.
Localized bruising, swelling, and point tenderness usually are present in patients with an acute
injury.
The clinician should assess the entirety of the clavicle and the sternoclavicular joint for
swelling, deformity, and tenderness.
Range of motion (ROM) and strength of the rotator cuff typically are normal in patients with
chronic injuries but may be limited in patients with an acute injury secondary to pain.
If the acromioclavicular joint is not reducible via the direct application of force on the distal
clavicle, an interposition of fascia or cartilage may be present and may be an indication for
surgical management.7
Horizontal plane translation of the distal clavicle should be assessed manually and compared
with that of the opposite shoulder.
A complete neurologic examination of the upper extremity should be performed to rule out
brachial plexus injuries.
Scapular motion should be carefully assessed and any dyskinesia should be noted.

Point tenderness is observed at the acromioclavicular joint, which is associated with a reported
sensitivity of 96% for acromioclavicular joint pathology.
The cross-body adduction test, in which pain over the acromioclavicular joint is generated by
maximal passive shoulder adduction at 90° of forward elevation, is associated with a reported
sensitivity of 67%.9
The O’Brien test primarily is designed to detect superior labral tears but also can be used in
diagnosis of the acromioclavicular joint pathology and is associated with a reported specificity
of 83% to 90%.9 In the O’Brien test, the patient is asked to bring the arm to 15° of adduction
and 90° of elevation and resist downward pressure on the arm while the arm is internally
rotated. The test is considered positive if the maneuver generates pain over the
acromioclavicular joint that is lessened by external rotation.
The acromioclavicular joint should be examined for deformity.
Selective injection of anesthetic into the acromioclavicular joint can confirm the diagnosis.
Distal Clavicle Osteolysis
Physical examination findings include localized pain, swelling, and tenderness, similar to that
observed in patients with symptomatic acromioclavicular joint arthritis.
Neurovascular Examination
A complete neurologic examination of the upper extremity should be performed to rule out
brachial plexus injuries.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Plain radiographs include an AP view of the clavicle, a caudal tilt view, and an axillary view.
A Zanca view (a modified, underpenetrated AP view with cephalic tilt of 10° to 15°) provides
excellent detail of the distal clavicle.10
Bilateral panoramic radiographs with digitally measured coracoclavicular distance provide the
most accurate assessment of the vertical stability of the acromioclavicular joint. No consensus
exists with regard to the best imaging modality for assessing horizontal stability of the

12/25

acromioclavicular joint; however, an axillary view will help to rule out posterior translation of
the distal clavicle.10
Weight-bearing views are difficult to obtain in the acute setting and often are not clinically
helpful.10
Osteoarthritis
Plain radiographs of the shoulder, including an AP view and/or a Zanca view, provide good
visualization of the acromioclavicular joint to assess for arthritic changes.
Distal Clavicle Osteolysis
Plain radiographs, including an AP view and/or a Zanca view, may reveal osteolysis and bone
resorption of the distal clavicle.

Radiography
Bilateral panoramic radiographs with digitally measured coracoclavicular distance
provide the most accurate assessment of the vertical stability of the acromioclavicular
joint.10 A normal coracoclavicular distance (between the superior aspect of the coracoid
and the inferior clavicle) is between 11 and 13 mm. No consensus exists with regard to
the best imaging modality for assessing horizontal stability of the acromioclavicular joint.
An axillary view helps rule out posterior translation of the distal clavicle. The anterior
aspect of the clavicle should lie in the same plane as the anterior aspect of the acromion.
Fracture of the base of the coracoid process also should be ruled out. A coracoid
fracture may result in superior displacement of the clavicle but an intact coracoclavicular
distance, creating a functionally equivalent acromioclavicular joint separation. A Zanca
view (a modified, underpenetrated AP view with cephalic tilt of 10° to 15°) provides
excellent detail of the distal clavicle. Weight-bearing views include bilateral AP views with
a weight tied to the wrists in relaxed standing. They help distinguish between type II and
type III separations but rarely are indicated and often are not clinically helpful.10

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Osteoarthritis
Bone and joint edema observed on MRI may better correlate with acromioclavicular joint pain
than highly prevalent changes observed on plain radiographs.
Distal Clavicle Osteolysis
Bone edema and distal clavicle osteolysis may be more accurately detected via MRI than via
plain radiography.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Plain radiographs of the shoulder of patients with acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis
may commonly demonstrate joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, sclerotic
reaction, and subchondral bone cysts; however, acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis is a
ubiquitous finding on imaging studies, and patients may not be symptomatic.11 Some
studies suggest that MRI showing distal clavicle bone edema or subchondral fracture or
cysts may be more closely correlated with symptomatic acromioclavicular joint
arthritis.11-13 Similarly, MRI may more accurately reveal the extent of bone edema and
osteolysis in patients with distal clavicle osteolysis than plain radiography alone.5
Overall, imaging findings must be closely correlated with physical examination findings
in patients with acromioclavicular joint arthritis because of the prevalence of
acromioclavicular joint arthritis in the population.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Indications
Nonsurgical management is recommended for type I and type II injuries. Good functional
outcomes can be expected.

9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Acromioclavicular Joint Arthritis and Pathology
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000631
14/25

Contraindications
Nonsurgical management is likely to fail in type IV, type V, and type VI injuries, resulting in pain
and limited function.
Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management of acromioclavicular separations consists of initial sling
immobilization followed by gradual active ROM exercises and stretching, followed by
strengthening as tolerated.
The recommended treatment option (surgical versus nonsurgical) for type III injuries is
controversial and depends on patient age and activity level.
Osteoarthritis
Nonsurgical management—Rest, ice, and NSAIDs are used initially; corticosteroid injections
also can be used for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes.
Distal Clavicle Osteolysis
Nonsurgical management includes rest, NSAIDs, ice, activity modifications, and corticosteroid
injections.

Nonsurgical Management
Most patients treated nonsurgically regain full shoulder function within 4 to 6 weeks
postinjury; however, they have an increased risk for future painful acromioclavicular
joint arthritis. Research indicates that between 30% and 50% of young, very active
patients will have mild to moderate residual pain at the acromioclavicular joint.14 The
recommended treatment option for type III injuries is controversial and depends on
patient age and activity level. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews demonstrate similar
outcomes between type III separations managed nonsurgically versus surgically. A
prospective, randomized trial of type III and type V injuries reported better results with

nonsurgical management if clavicle displacement was less than 2 cm and better results
with surgical management if clavicle displacement was more than 2 cm.15
Surgical Management
Indications
Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Surgical management is indicated for most acute type IV, type V, and type VI separations.
Surgical management is indicated in select type III separations.

Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Acute type IV, type V, and type VI separations should be managed surgically; however,
some controversy exists with regard to the surgical management of select type III
injuries.14,16 Surgical management may be indicated for select type III separations in
younger, physically active patients; manual laborers; patients with cosmetic concerns;
and patients with chronic injuries who have persistent symptoms. In addition, some
surgeons acutely manage type IIIB (horizontally unstable) separations surgically.14
Osteoarthritis
Surgical indications include persistent pain and failed nonsurgical management.
Distal Clavicle Osteolysis
Indications are persistent pain despite nonsurgical management.
Contraindications
Osteoarthritis
Relative contraindication may include a previous acromioclavicular separation with persistent
horizontal plane instability.

Techniques/Procedures
Surgical Approaches
Acromioclavicular joint separation
Numerous surgical techniques had been described to manage acromioclavicular separations;
however, no consensus exists with regard to the best reconstructive option.
The Weaver-Dunn procedure
The classic Weaver-Dunn procedure involved distal clavicle excision and coracoacromial
ligament transfer; it was associated with more than 30% persistent instability and currently
is less commonly performed.17
The modified Weaver-Dunn procedure involves additional coracoclavicular fixation with the
use of a suture, surgical tape, cerclage wire, allograft tendon, or screw to maintain
coracoclavicular reduction17,18 Video 1.
Video 1

Acromioclavicular Joint Dislocation [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic

September 30, 2022.
Hook plates can be used to manage acromioclavicular joint separations and distal clavicle
fractures with coracoclavicular ligament disruption.

Modern management of acromioclavicular joint separations involves anatomic
reconstruction of the coracoclavicular ligaments via a suspensory-type fixation, with the
possible addition of acromioclavicular capsule reconstruction and graft augmentation.18
Surgical reconstruction delayed more than 3 weeks may benefit from a biologic
augmentation, commonly in the form of a tendon graft.
Distal clavicle excision can be performed in combination with acromioclavicular joint
reconstruction if the deformity is not fully reducible.
Two studies compared the results of coracoclavicular reconstruction with and without
distal clavicle resection and did not report any difference in radiographic failure and
complications between the two groups.18,19
To avoid destabilization of the acromioclavicular joint, the size of the resection should be
less than 10 mm.18
Anatomic reconstruction of the coracoclavicular ligaments can be accomplished via various
fixation techniques.
Suspensory fixation and/or the tendon graft can be passed around the coracoid base and
distal clavicle and secured with the use of suture alone.
Alternatively, some combination of drilling tunnels through the distal clavicle and/or
coracoid base can be used for suspensory fixation and graft passage/fixation. Fixation
methods for the tunnels include titanium button devices, suture anchors, or interference
screws.
Osteoarthritis
Arthroscopic versus open distal clavicle excision
Resection between 5 and 10 mm is necessary to prevent contact between the clavicle and
the acromion.
Care should be taken to preserve the posterior and superior acromioclavicular joint
ligaments.
Open distal clavicle resection (Mumford procedure)
Between 5 and 10 mm of the distal clavicle should be respected.
Good repair of the deltotrapezial fascia is important.
Distal clavicle osteolysis—Options include arthroscopic or open distal clavicle excision.

Surgical Approaches

Hook plates were initially used for the management of distal clavicle fractures with
coracoclavicular ligament injury and currently have been applied to acromioclavicular
joint separations, with results equivalent to those of nonsurgical management; however,
they may lead to acromial erosion and rotator cuff irritation. Because of these concerns,
the use of hook plates requires close patient follow-up because they should be removed
after healing has occurred.20 Currently, most surgical treatment options for
acromioclavicular joint separations involve anatomic reconstruction of the
coracoclavicular ligaments via a suspensory type fixation with the possible addition of
acromioclavicular joint capsule reconstruction and graft augmentation, depending on
the timing and extent of injury.18 Acute injuries have a high potential for healing of the
coracoclavicular ligaments, allowing for reconstruction via techniques that hold the
acromioclavicular joint in anatomic reduction as ligament healing occurs.21 For
reconstructions occurring more than 3 weeks postinjury, biologic augmentation often is
used.22 Most reconstruction techniques involve the use of tendon allografts; however,
autografts also have been described. The most commonly used autograft or allograft is
semitendinosus; however, the use of peroneus longus, tibialis anterior, palmaris longus,
and gracilis has been reported.23
Biomechanical evidence suggests a resection of 5 mm is necessary to prevent contact
between the distal clavicle and acromion. Care should be taken to preserve the posterior
and superior acromioclavicular joint ligaments to prevent future instability. Studies have
shown that resection greater than 1 cm may lead to acromioclavicular joint instability.24
Pain relief is reliable (in >90% of patients) in the absence of instability; however, previous
traumatic instability is associated with persistent pain in a small portion of patients after
distal clavicle excision. Research has shown good outcomes after arthroscopic and open
distal clavicle excision.25

Complications
Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
Nonsurgical management of type III through type V acromioclavicular joint separation may
result in persistent pain, acromioclavicular joint instability, and scapular dyskinesia.27
Overall, the rate of serious complications remains low with modern acromioclavicular joint
reconstruction techniques.28
The most common complication after acromioclavicular joint reconstruction is loss of
reduction, which occurs in 20% of patients, commonly during the first 6 weeks

The reported infection rate is 3.8% and is higher in patients who undergo open

Coracoid and/or clavicle fracture are reported in 5.3% of patients and are associated with

Hook plates have been associated with hook pullout and acromial erosion.
Any technique that involves the passage of a graft or synthetic material medial to the coracoid
process poses a risk for brachial plexus injury.
Osteoarthritis and Distal Clavicle Osteolysis
Wide resection of the distal clavicle beyond 10 mm increases the risk of compromising the
coracoclavicular ligament attachment and may result in iatrogenic acromioclavicular joint
instability.30
